lesson.title: The Bellman Ford Algorithm: The Math Behind Distance Vector Routing
lesson.summary: The Bellman Ford algorithm is the classic shortest path algorithm whose update rule, repeatedly improve a distance estimate using a neighbor's estimate plus the connecting link cost, is exactly what real distance vector routers run in a distributed, ongoing form.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter's update rule, look at what each neighbor advertises, add the cost of reaching that neighbor, and keep whichever option is cheapest, is not something networking invented from scratch. It is a direct application of the Bellman Ford algorithm, a general method from graph theory for finding shortest paths, developed independently by Richard Bellman and Lester Ford in the 1950s, that works even on graphs with a mix of edge costs, as long as there is no cycle whose total cost is negative, not a concern for routing, where link costs are never negative.

Bellman Ford's core operation is usually called relaxation: for a candidate shortest path estimate to some node y, check whether going through some neighboring node v would be cheaper, and if so, replace the estimate with the cheaper one. Written as an equation, the distance from x to y is the minimum, over all neighbors v, of the cost from x to v plus the distance from v to y. Run that check enough times, across enough nodes, and the estimates provably converge to the true shortest paths. What makes it a good fit for routing is that the algorithm does not need to see the whole graph at once, it only ever needs local information, a node's own link costs and its neighbors' current distance estimates, which is exactly the information a router naturally has.

Return to the X, Y, Z example from the last chapter to see the convergence property in action. After the first exchange, X's distance to Z dropped from 7 to 3, by way of Y, and Z's distance to X dropped from 7 to 3, by way of Y as well. If X and Z now exchange vectors again, does anything else improve. X already believes the true shortest path to Z, 3, so a further update through Z's newly improved vector does not find anything cheaper. The same holds for every other pairing in this small network. Once no router can find a cheaper path by relaxing against its neighbors' current advertisements, the algorithm has converged, and the routing tables describe the true shortest paths.

One important difference from the textbook version of Bellman Ford is timing. A classical graph algorithm typically runs to completion on a fixed input. Real networks are never that tidy: routers send updates on their own schedules, links go up and down, and a router can receive a neighbor's vector at any moment. This asynchronous, always running version of Bellman Ford is generally well behaved when link costs only ever get cheaper or the network is stable, but, as the next chapter shows, it has a genuine weak spot when a link's cost gets worse or a link disappears entirely.
